code.title: Pass by value, reference and const reference

followUps: Because a plain int already fits in one CPU register, while a reference is really an 8-byte address that must be passed and then followed to reach the value. On a 64-bit machine the int is only 4 bytes, so the reference is not smaller, and each use adds a memory load. It can also force the compiler to assume the value might change through another name and re-read it. Rule of thumb: types up to about two machine words (int, double, pointers, string_view) go by value.

A sink parameter is one the function will keep or store, so it takes it by value and moves it into place. Example: void setName(std::string n) { name = std::move(n); }. If the caller passes a temporary, the cost is one move; if the caller passes a named string, it is one copy plus one move. A const std::string& version would always copy, and writing both const& and && overloads doubles the code. The price of the by-value way is one extra cheap move.

Java always passes by value, but for objects the value that is copied is the reference itself. So the method can change the object's fields and the caller sees it, yet assigning a new object to the parameter does not affect the caller. C++ lets you choose: void f(Foo& x) { x = Foo(); } replaces the caller's object, which Java cannot do, and a const T& parameter promises not to modify it, which Java has no equivalent for. A classic swap(a, b) works in C++ and cannot be written in Java.

code.title: Reference aliasing versus a re-pointable pointer

followUps: You cannot have a reference to a reference or an array of references, because a reference is only an alias and is not a separate object with its own storage. If templates produce T&& through a typedef, reference collapsing simply folds it into one reference. To keep several references in a container use std::reference_wrapper, for example vector<reference_wrapper<int>> v = {a, b};, or an array of pointers. Writing v[0].get() = 5 then changes a.

A dangling reference is one that still names an object that has already been destroyed, so using it is undefined behaviour. Three common ways to create one: returning a reference to a local (int& f() { int x = 5; return x; }), keeping a reference to a vector element and then calling push_back that reallocates, and binding a long-lived reference to a temporary that dies at the end of the statement. The program may print the old value, garbage or crash. The fix is to return by value, keep an index, or make sure the object outlives the reference.

code.title: vector size, capacity and geometric growth

followUps: After a reallocation every pointer, reference and iterator into the vector is invalidated, including end(), because all elements moved to a new buffer. Without a reallocation (size below capacity) a push_back invalidates only end(), and an insert in the middle invalidates everything from the insertion point on. Example: v = {1,2} has capacity 2, so after p = &v[0]; v.push_back(3); the pointer p dangles. Fix: keep indices, or call reserve before taking pointers.

Because a throwing move can leave the old buffer half empty, and then the vector can no longer give its strong exception guarantee. With a copy, if element 7 of 10 throws, the old buffer is still intact and the new one is thrown away. So push_back uses std::move_if_noexcept: it moves only when the move constructor is noexcept (or when copying is impossible). The practical lesson: mark your move constructors and move assignments noexcept, otherwise vector growth silently copies every element.

With factor 2 a new block (size 2c) can never fit in the space freed by earlier blocks: capacities 1, 2, 4, 8 free 1+2+4 = 7 bytes-units, which is always less than the next request of 8, so the allocator cannot reuse that memory. With a factor below the golden ratio (about 1.618), such as 1.5, the freed blocks eventually add up to enough for the next one, so memory can be recycled and cache behaviour improves. The cost is a few more reallocations, but total copying is still at most 3n, so push_back stays amortised O(1).

code.title: Array-to-pointer decay and the fixes

followUps: An array does not decay when it is the operand of sizeof, of unary &, of decltype, or when it is bound to a reference or template parameter of array type, and when a char array is initialised from a string literal. Example: with int a[10], sizeof(a) is 40 (not 8), &a has type int(*)[10], and void f(int (&r)[10]) keeps the length in the type. Every other use, such as passing to a function or adding 1, turns it into int*.

std::span<T> (C++20) is a non-owning view of contiguous memory: just a pointer plus a length (16 bytes), cheap to pass by value. It accepts C arrays, std::array and vector alike, and span<const int> makes it read-only. It does not own anything: it never frees or grows the data, and it dangles if the underlying vector reallocates or is destroyed. Example: int sum(std::span<const int> s) works for sum(vec) and sum(arr) without copying.

code.title: Overload resolution: which f is called

followUps: Because the compiler picks the function from the arguments alone, before it knows what will be done with the result, and the result may even be thrown away. With int f(int) and double f(int) the call f(1); is identical for both, so it would be ambiguous. Overload on parameter types instead, use different names, or choose by an explicit template argument, for example template<class R> R conv(int) called as conv<double>(1).

Name mangling is how the compiler encodes the parameter types into the symbol name, so overloads get different linker names: f(int) may become _Z1fi and f(double) becomes _Z1fd in GCC. extern "C" switches that off and uses the plain C name, so C code can link against the function and the other way round. The consequence is that you cannot overload extern "C" functions, since two functions would get the same symbol. Example: extern "C" int add(int, int);.

Function templates join the candidate list after type deduction, and are ranked with the same conversion rules. If a template and an ordinary function are equally good, the non-template wins. With void f(int) and template<class T> void f(T), f(5) calls the plain int version, but f(5.0) calls the template with T = double because that is an exact match while the int version needs a conversion. Templates whose substitution fails (SFINAE) or whose concept is not satisfied simply drop out of the set.

code.title: Default arguments, including on virtual functions

followUps: The default value is chosen from the static type (the declared type of the pointer or reference), while the function body that runs is chosen from the dynamic type. So with Base::f(int x = 1) and Derived::f(int x = 2), a call base_ptr->f() on a Derived object runs Derived's body with x = 1. That surprises people, so never give an override a different default. If you need a default on a virtual, use a non-virtual public wrapper that supplies it and calls the virtual function.

Prefer overloads when the missing argument needs different logic, not just a constant, or when the default must be computed from the other arguments. They also keep the default out of every caller's compiled code, so you can change the behaviour without recompiling callers, and they avoid ambiguity traps. Example: print(int v) and print(int v, int width) can call different code paths, while one function with width = 0 would need a branch inside. Defaults are best for a simple constant such as bool verbose = false.

code.title: Deep recursion versus an explicit stack

followUps: A local variable lives in its function's frame, and that frame is popped when the function returns. The memory is then reused by the next call, so the pointer refers to dead storage and using it is undefined behaviour. Example: int* f() { int x = 7; return &x; } may print 7 right away, then garbage after another function call overwrites the spot. Fix it by returning the value, by passing a buffer in, or by allocating on the heap with std::make_unique.

Tail-call optimisation means that when the last action of a function is a call, the compiler reuses the current frame and jumps instead of calling, so recursion uses O(1) stack. C++ does not guarantee it: GCC and Clang usually do it at -O2 but not at -O0, and a local with a destructor still pending stops the call from being in tail position. So do not rely on it for deep recursion. Write the loop instead: long s = 0; while (n > 0) { s += n; --n; }.

code.title: Classic C++ loop bugs and safe loops

followUps: Use an unsigned-safe pattern: for (size_t i = v.size(); i-- > 0; ) use(v[i]);. The test runs before the decrement takes effect inside the body, so for size 3 the body sees i = 2, 1, 0 and then stops, and an empty vector skips the loop at once. Alternatives are reverse iterators, for (auto it = v.rbegin(); it != v.rend(); ++it), or C++20 std::views::reverse. The tempting for (size_t i = n - 1; i >= 0; --i) never ends.

A loop invariant is a statement that is true before the loop and after every iteration, so when the loop ends it gives you the result. For binary search the invariant is: if the target is in the array, it lies in [lo, hi]. It is true at the start (lo = 0, hi = n - 1), each step throws away only the half that cannot hold the target, and when lo > hi the range is empty, so the target is absent. Example: {1,3,5,7}, target 5: mid = 1 (3 < 5) so lo = 2; then mid = 2 finds it.

code.title: C array vs std::array vs vector

followUps: A std::array stores its elements inside the object itself, so it lives wherever the object lives: a local variable is on the stack, a global is in static storage, and a member of a heap object is on the heap. That is why a large std::array<int, 10000000> local (40 MB) overflows the stack, while the same size vector is fine, because the vector keeps only a 24-byte header locally and its elements on the heap.

vector<bool> is a special version that packs one bit per element, so it is not a normal container of bools. operator[] returns a proxy object instead of bool&, so bool* p = &v[0] does not compile, auto x = v[0] gets a proxy, there is no data(), and neighbouring bits share bytes so threads can race. It saves 8 times the memory of vector<char>. Use vector<char>, vector<uint8_t> or std::bitset<N> when you need real elements.

code.title: SSO, embedded NUL and UTF-8 bytes

followUps: string_view is a non-owning pair of pointer and length over characters that live somewhere else. It adds cheap, copy-free parameters and slicing: substr is O(1) and it accepts literals, std::string and char arrays alike. The main danger is dangling: if the original string is destroyed, modified or reallocated the view points at dead memory, for example string_view sv = string("hi") + "!"; refers to a temporary. It is also not guaranteed null-terminated. Use it for function parameters, not for storing.

Because std::string counts bytes (chars), not characters, and it knows nothing about encodings. In a UTF-8 source file the letter é is stored as two bytes, 0xC3 0xA9, so size() is 2; an emoji takes 4 bytes. To count code points, count the bytes that are not continuation bytes: (b & 0xC0) != 0x80. Counting user-visible characters needs a Unicode library such as ICU.

code.title: s = s + c versus s += c

followUps: Rarely, so do not count on it. s + c with a named s must produce a new string, and compilers almost never rewrite that into an in-place append, because they would have to prove that nothing else sees s in between. Write s += c. You can write s = std::move(s) + c, since operator+ on an rvalue string appends in place, but += says the same thing more clearly.

Add up the sizes first, reserve once, then append each piece, so the cost is O(total characters) with a single allocation. Example: size_t t = sep.size() * (n - 1); for (auto& p : parts) t += p.size(); out.reserve(t); for (i...) { if (i) out += sep; out += parts[i]; }. An ostringstream works too, and C++23 offers views::join_with. Avoid out = out + p + sep in the loop, which is quadratic.

code.title: switch fallthrough and leaving nested loops

followUps: C++ has no multi-level break, so pick one of three ways. Best: move the loops into a function or lambda and return as soon as you have the answer. Second: set a bool done flag and check it in the outer loop condition. Third: goto end; to a label after the loops, which is acceptable here and clear. Example: auto found = [&] { for (...) for (...) if (ok) return true; return false; }(); stops both loops at the first match.

A switch needs integral or enum constants known at compile time, since it is compiled into a jump table or binary search over integers. A std::string is not an integer and its comparison is not a compile-time constant. Common workarounds: an if / else if chain using ==; a std::unordered_map<string, Handler> that maps the text to a function; or map the string to an enum once and then switch on the enum. For a few cases the if-chain is clearest.

code.title: Reallocation invalidates references

followUps: Yes, the standard requires v.push_back(v[0]) to work even if it reallocates, because implementations must build the new element before releasing the old buffer. With v = {1, 2} it gives {1, 2, 1}. This only covers the argument of the call itself. A reference r that you stored before the call still dangles after a reallocation, so the rule is: the argument is safe, any other earlier reference is not.

std::list, map, set and the unordered containers never move their elements, so pointers and references to them stay valid on insertion (an unordered container may invalidate iterators on rehash, but not references). Only an erased element becomes invalid. std::deque keeps references valid when you push at either end, but invalidates iterators, and an insert in the middle invalidates everything. A vector is the container with the weakest guarantee because it reallocates.

code.title: Returning several values: struct, pair, optional, out-param

followUps: NRVO (named return value optimisation) lets the compiler build a named local directly in the caller's return slot, so no copy or move happens. It cannot apply when different named locals are returned on different paths (if (c) return a; else return b;), when you return a parameter, member or global, or when you write return std::move(x); which actually blocks it. It is not guaranteed for named locals (only unnamed temporaries are guaranteed since C++17), but then the compiler falls back to a cheap move.

An output parameter is still right when you reuse a big buffer across many calls: void readLine(std::istream& in, std::string& line) keeps the string's capacity, so a loop reading a million lines allocates only a few times, where returning a fresh string would allocate each time. It also fits when you fill memory that the caller owns (a span or array), when matching a C API, or when the function returns a status code and the data separately. In normal code, return by value.
